hook: I spent $34 instead of $500 on my Christmas tree

scenes.visual_prompt: Close shot of a bare-looking 7.5-foot artificial tree, ornaments clustered unevenly, big gaps between branches
scenes.on_screen_text: This tree cost me nothing to look bad
scenes.voiceover: My tree had 40 ornaments on it and still looked empty.

scenes.visual_prompt: Hand holds a $34 velvet ribbon and ornament bundle box next to a printed quote for professional tree styling
scenes.voiceover: A professional tree stylist in most markets runs $300 to $600, plus a takedown fee in January.

scenes.visual_prompt: Close-up of warm-white string lights being threaded into the interior branches of the tree, not just the tips
scenes.voiceover: Reviewers kept flagging the same fix: warm-white lights pushed deep into the tree, not just wrapped around the outside.

scenes.visual_prompt: Velvet ribbon spiraling diagonally down the tree, secured with a small wire twist every 12-18 inches
scenes.voiceover: The ribbon spirals diagonally, top to base, offset so it never reads like a candy cane.

scenes.visual_prompt: Hands wiring three ornaments together, one large one medium one small, at a single branch point
scenes.voiceover: Ornaments go on in clusters of three — that's the part most people skip, and it's why the bundle still looks sparse otherwise.

scenes.visual_prompt: Camera pulls back to reveal the fully layered, full-looking tree next to a small matching birch accent tree
scenes.voiceover: Add a $19.99 accent tree for the entryway and I'm at roughly $94 total for both.

scenes.visual_prompt: Split screen, bare tree on left, finished styled tree on right, text overlay with price comparison
scenes.voiceover: Link's in my bio if you want the exact bundle I used.

caption: I almost paid a stylist $500 to fix my tree. Then I did the math on a $34 ribbon bundle instead. Breaking down exactly what's in it, what has to go on first, and why the ornament math actually matters — full writeup on the blog.
